screenings.title: Filipiñana
screenings.description: “A masterwork—which is all the more remarkable given that it’s the first feature by the Filipino director Rafael Manuel... The film performs a scalpel-sharp dissection of the [luxury tourism] industry, laying bare a mad microcosm of power relations—political, sexual, economic, familial, cultural, even linguistic—and the aesthetic of dominance that the resort, in Manuel’s discerning view, projects... Manuel’s approach to narrative is as original as his sense of cinematic form, and his gift for documentary-style observation is balanced by a refined sense of style.” – Richard Brody, The New Yorker “Darkly comic, visually inventive... cinematically builds into a scathing account of inequality, showing how women like Isabel are condemned to work in a place whose atmosphere is closer to that of a colonial plantation than a cushy country club.” – Jordan Mintzer, The Hollywood Reporter “An invigorating dose of arch formalism in a sea of mainstream sincerity, this is the kind of movie that asks for the viewer’s attention and patience—not because it is slow or oblique but because it’s built entirely out of details... the angle of a golf club can evoke suspense, a piece of fruit on the ground can feel like a tragedy, and a casual glance can take your breath away.” – Bilge Ebiri, Vulture “Manuel uses his fastidiously arranged tableaux to give a tension and dark sense of humor to his fiery vision of Filipino high society. Set in an eerily well-manicured golf course outside Manila, this deadpan drama, with the symmetrical style of a Wes Anderson movie, patiently snakes its way through the club’s inner workings.” – Beatrice Loayza, The New York Times ★★★★ “Brilliantly biting... In a year of several standout debuts, Manuel’s ranks among the most impressive. The microcosm he meticulously constructs makes for a rivetingly caustic indictment of his homeland.” – Carlos Aguilar, RogerEbert.com

screenings.description: On a remote Scottish isle, siblings Isla (Gayle Rankin, GLOW) and Sandy (Grant O’Rourke, Outlander) spend their days hunting seabirds and retelling the stories of their ancestors. They follow the strict rules inherited from their late father — protect the island, allow no incomer, survive — until one day, Daniel (Domhnall Gleeson, Ex Machina), an awkward and socially inept council official, arrives to evacuate them. Bringing with him the strange mainland ways of laws, paperwork, veganism and internet wizardry, he turns their world upside down.

screenings.title: The Sun Never Sets
screenings.description: Free-spirited Wendy (Dakota Fanning) is at a crossroads in her relationship with older divorced dad Jack (Jake Johnson, New Girl) that is only further complicated when an old flame (Cory Michael Smith, Sentimental Value) re-enters her life. Set in perpetually sunny summertime Anchorage and featuring a career-best performance by Fanning, THE SUN NEVER SETS is a funny and endearing return to form for mumblecore auteur Joe Swanberg.

Detecting his brother’s exceptional musical talent, he takes it upon himself to rectify the injustice of fate. An equally hilarious and affecting crowdpleaser that premiered at Cannes and became a French box office sensation starring Benjamin Lavernhe (My Donkey, My Lover & I) and Pierre Lottin (The Stranger). screenings.title: In Spite of Ourselves
screenings.description: Love comes easy — relationships don’t. When Hannah, a warm and determined Portland, Oregon baker, crosses paths with Archie, an up-and-coming L.A. comedian with a habit of dodging commitment, their instant chemistry sparks a whirlwind romance neither expected. But after two blissful weeks together real life pulls them back to separate cities – forcing them to confront distance, doubts, and their own hilariously messy insecurities.

screenings.title: Tender Loving Care
screenings.description: Dir. Mike Leigh. 2026, 107 mins. U.K. DCP. One of our most steadfast, unflinching chroniclers of the human condition, Mike Leigh has now crafted, along with a customarily brilliant ensemble, a portrayal of overwhelmed, resilient lives in post-Brexit England that should be received as one of his signature works. At its center is Amy (Kate O’Flynn), a government child protection worker who, after a failed relationship, has moved back in with her chipper best friend, Rosie (Alice Bailey Johnson), whose job as a social services officer is a daily confrontation with anger and resentment. Meanwhile, Amy’s aging parents (Marion Bailey and Paul Jesson), concerned with their daughter’s happiness, suddenly have to contend with a crisis of their own. Smiling through their struggles—with or without a trusty bottle of wine—these finely drawn characters, and all of the remarkable supporting characters with whom they come into contact, speak volumes about the U.K.’s underfunded and fragmented care sector. Avoiding didacticism and maintaining a leveling sense of humor, Leigh shows, with clear-eyed compassion, the difficulty of asking for—and accepting—help in a world that continually lets us down. screenings.title: Atonement (2026)
screenings.language: English and Arabic with English Subtitles
screenings.description: Displaced from their home by U.S. military action during the early days of the Iraq War, the Khachaturian family finds refuge with relatives, gathering their three generations together under one roof. But when another bombing erupts nearby, they decide to return to their home across the city. As they navigate the war-torn streets of Baghdad, the family is trapped in a firefight between U.S. Marines and insurgents, and one Marine’s split-second decision devastates the family. Years later, haunted by his time in Iraq and aided by a New Yorker journalist, the Marine seeks to reconcile with the Khachaturian matriarch and her surviving family members. Anchored by moving, unforgettable performances from Boyd Holbrook, Hiam Abbass, and Kenneth Branagh, Atonement is a powerfully human story about the immeasurable costs of war, exploring universal questions about guilt, redemption, and the nature of forgiveness.

screenings.title: You Had to Be There
screenings.description: “AN EXUBERANT AND ESSENTIAL DOC FOR COMEDY HEADS... The comedy revolution referred to by the title of Nick Davis’s sharp and effusive documentary YOU HAD TO BE THERE: HOW THE TORONTO GODSPELL IGNITED THE COMEDY REVOLUTION... is the one that took place on television in the ’70s: the creation of Saturday Night Live and SCTV and everything that grew out of them. YOU HAD TO BE THERE makes the case that the Petri dish from which the DNA of those shows was sprung was the 1972 Toronto production of Godspell, the Jesus-and-his-followers-as-hippie-clowns musical that had rocked the world when it premiered on Broadway the year before. The Toronto production featured a young Martin Short, Eugene Levy, Andrea Martin, Dave Thomas (all Canadian), and, from across the river, Detroit’s own Gilda Radner—who was the very first performer to be cast on Saturday Night, a show created by Lorne Michaels, who was also Canadian... There’s passionate testimony from the likes of Mike Myers and Lin-Manuel Miranda, who hails the show as ‘the ’27 Yankees of comedy.’ YOU HAD TO BE THERE shows you that something was in the air up there, and that it spread like the world’s happiest virus.” – Owen Gleiberman, Variety “Director Nick Davis’ terrific return to this historic event offers a laugh-a-minute trip down memory lane that’s not merely nostalgic. It’s a valuable oral history of a defining moment in pop culture... A hugely entertaining record of Canadian cultural history worthy of time and celebration. And, in perhaps the most Canadian trait ever, it’s an American production.” – Pat Mullen, POV Magazine

screenings.title: Danton
screenings.description: France/Poland, 1983 Directed by Andrzej Wajda Written by Jean-Claude Carrière, Wajda, Agnieszka Holland Starring Gérard Depardieu, Wojciech Pszoniak, Anne Alvaro Approx. 136 mins. Based on The Danton Affair, a 1930s play that Wajda directed on stage in 1975, this boisterous and lavish French production starring Gerard Depardieu and scripted by Jean-Claude Carriere, may have seemed like a break from contemporary Polish politics. But Depardieu’s Danton, an earthy, plain-spoken man of the people, was widely seen as a representation of Polish solidarity leader Lech Walesa, and Wojciech Pszoniak’s reserved, cerebral Robespierre, was seen as the iron-fisted military general and Polish president Wojciech Jaruzelski. The film’s politics have been widely debated, but the movie, a rare Wajda production made outside of his own country, was a hit of the 1983 New York Film Festival and an arthouse success. Presented with support from The Ashes and Diamonds Fund for Eastern European Film and The Ada Katz Fund for Literature in Film

screenings.title: Deep Red
screenings.description: Anticipating the eerie magic of Suspiria, Deep Red finds Dario Argento and creative partner Daria Nicolodi presenting a simple, Christmas-set slasher. At least, that’s what it appears to be. But within two minutes, it’s obvious that there’s nothing “simple” about Deep Red at all. With this movie, Argento perfected the classy, ultra-violent sub-genre that would come to be known as giallo—and also perfected playing audiences like a fiddle. This includes Goblin’s soundtrack, which is a spook-a-delic prog-rock masterpiece that beautifully complements the movie’s dreamy mood.

screenings.title: Filipiñana
screenings.description: “A masterwork—which is all the more remarkable given that it’s the first feature by the Filipino director Rafael Manuel... The film performs a scalpel-sharp dissection of the [luxury tourism] industry, laying bare a mad microcosm of power relations—political, sexual, economic, familial, cultural, even linguistic—and the aesthetic of dominance that the resort, in Manuel’s discerning view, projects... Manuel’s approach to narrative is as original as his sense of cinematic form, and his gift for documentary-style observation is balanced by a refined sense of style.” – Richard Brody, The New Yorker “Darkly comic, visually inventive... cinematically builds into a scathing account of inequality, showing how women like Isabel are condemned to work in a place whose atmosphere is closer to that of a colonial plantation than a cushy country club.” – Jordan Mintzer, The Hollywood Reporter “An invigorating dose of arch formalism in a sea of mainstream sincerity, this is the kind of movie that asks for the viewer’s attention and patience—not because it is slow or oblique but because it’s built entirely out of details... the angle of a golf club can evoke suspense, a piece of fruit on the ground can feel like a tragedy, and a casual glance can take your breath away.” – Bilge Ebiri, Vulture “Manuel uses his fastidiously arranged tableaux to give a tension and dark sense of humor to his fiery vision of Filipino high society. Set in an eerily well-manicured golf course outside Manila, this deadpan drama, with the symmetrical style of a Wes Anderson movie, patiently snakes its way through the club’s inner workings.” – Beatrice Loayza, The New York Times ★★★★ “Brilliantly biting... In a year of several standout debuts, Manuel’s ranks among the most impressive. The microcosm he meticulously constructs makes for a rivetingly caustic indictment of his homeland.” – Carlos Aguilar, RogerEbert.com

screenings.title: Bitter Christmas
screenings.description: Dir. Pedro Almodóvar. 2026, 111 mins. Spain. DCP. Spanish with English subtitles. The incomparable Almodóvar has been rendering the life of the creative mind on screen for five decades, with exquisite attention to every nuance of both aesthetic design and human emotion. With his complexly conceived latest, he uses a metacinematic framework to explore the artist’s tenuous relationship between fiction and reality. The sublimely expressive Bárbara Lennie stars as Elsa, a well-known actress suffering from debilitating migraines whose directorial efforts had failed upon release but have become cult classics. While trying to maintain a relationship with her loyal boyfriend Bonifacio (Patrick Criado), a fireman moonlighting as a stripper, she becomes inspired by the travails of her friends to write a new script. Yet Elsa’s story is itself a story—being written by Raúl (Leonardo Sbaraglia), an Almodóvar-esque filmmaker who is, in turn, taking his cues from the lives of those around him. Mixing the irreverence of early Almodóvar with the somber melodrama of his later work, Bitter Christmas insightfully details the vampiric nature of artistic creation and how we use fiction to try and right the wrongs of our lives. screenings.title: Ashes and Diamonds
screenings.description: Popiół i diament Poland, 1958 Directed by Andrzej Wajda Starring Zbigniew Cybulski, Ewa Krzyżewska, Wacław Zastrzeżyński Approx. 103 mins. 4K restoration/35mm. In the spring of 1945, weary and disillusioned by the war against the Nazis that has just ended, uncertain about a future under Communist rule, two resistance fighters are under orders to assassinate the incoming district leader. One of the fighters, the brooding Maciek, played by Zbigniew Cybulski (often called “the Polish James Dean”), falls in love with a local barmaid, and is suddenly torn about how to move forward. As Wajda said about ASHES AND DIAMONDS, almost universally regarded as his masterpiece, “I have tried to reveal to movie audiences the complicated and difficult world of a generation to which I myself belong.” This anguished, romantic, and deeply personal film is an all-time favorite of both Francis Ford Coppola and Martin Scorsese, who placed it as #3 on his top ten list for Sight and Sound. screenings.title: Naza
screenings.description: We made this film out of a sense of obligation to use our position as Israeli filmmakers and journalists to examine the systems behind the mass killing of Palestinian civilians for which our country is responsible. While filming members of Israel’s military on rooftops at night in Tel Aviv over the past three years, we found ourselves asking the very questions that were asked by our grandparents’ generation and throughout the 20th century: how does one group of people allow the total dehumanization of another? What do the inner workings of such a system look like? Many of the revelations in the film were published almost immediately as we learned of them, in the months following the October 7th attacks, by The Guardian (one of NAZA’s producers), in collaboration with reporting partners +972 Magazine and Local Call. The film lets us explore something deeper than we could in our investigative journalism alone: not only the words being said but also those that are not said, the silence. It is up to all of us to break that silence.

screenings.title: Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother in 35mm
screenings.description: From writer-director Bassam Tariq, YOUR MOTHER YOUR MOTHER YOUR MOTHER stars Mahershala Ali as Latif, a devoutly religious hitman who struggles to balance work, faith and fatherhood. When his wife dies, he embarks on a desperate journey across Houston to protect his children, confronting the forces closing in around him - and the beliefs threatening to unravel within.

screenings.title: Atonement (2026)
screenings.language: English and Arabic with English Subtitles
screenings.description: Displaced from their home by U.S. military action during the early days of the Iraq War, the Khachaturian family finds refuge with relatives, gathering their three generations together under one roof. But when another bombing erupts nearby, they decide to return to their home across the city. As they navigate the war-torn streets of Baghdad, the family is trapped in a firefight between U.S. Marines and insurgents, and one Marine’s split-second decision devastates the family. Years later, haunted by his time in Iraq and aided by a New Yorker journalist, the Marine seeks to reconcile with the Khachaturian matriarch and her surviving family members. Anchored by moving, unforgettable performances from Boyd Holbrook, Hiam Abbass, and Kenneth Branagh, Atonement is a powerfully human story about the immeasurable costs of war, exploring universal questions about guilt, redemption, and the nature of forgiveness.

screenings.title: Smart Girl (w/q&a)
screenings.description: In an attempt to one-up her smart sister, Hannah Lynn Crane copies her by writing a book. When she finds out her friend Barbara from Scrabble Group used to write romance novels, she enlists her help. Together they start brainstorming a daring age-gap romance novel, but when Barbara mysteriously disappears right before tackling the sex scenes, Hannah is left to her own devices. She falls down a dangerously addictive, GILF-riddled path to learn what being smart actually means.

screenings.title: Peaking: Psychedelics and the Pursuit of Happiness
screenings.description: PEAKING: PSYCHEDELICS AND THE PURSUIT OF HAPPINESS is a feature documentary that explores all the major psychedelics, not just by explaining how they work medicinally, but by taking viewers inside dosing rooms for extremely rare looks at the remarkable power, emotion, and speed of psychedelic healing in action: from pro athletes repairing brain damage from concussions, to combat veterans finding relief from suicidal despair, to a woman breaking free from opioid addiction, to survivors of the Nova Music Festival massacre who say being on psychedelics during the attack shielded them from developing mental trauma.

screenings.title: The Scout
screenings.description: Director González-Nasser spent six years working as a location scout. In this luminous directorial debut, she brings us into a day in the life of a young scout tasked with finding the perfect interiors for a television pilot. Sofía (Mimi Davila) moves in and out of other people’s intimate spaces and quotidian lives, tweaking her personality just enough to connect while struggling to find balance between her professional and personal worlds. With a mounting stack of parking tickets and the impertinent commentaries of her crew, she faces a series of small-yet-paralyzing obstacles that render her day increasingly exhausting. Through a constellation of quiet but poignant vignettes, the film offers an original view into the invisible labor of TV production, unfolding as an alternative symphony of a New York grappling with gentrification and a growing erosion of empathy. screenings.title: Danton
screenings.description: France/Poland, 1983 Directed by Andrzej Wajda Written by Jean-Claude Carrière, Wajda, Agnieszka Holland Starring Gérard Depardieu, Wojciech Pszoniak, Anne Alvaro Approx. 136 mins. Based on The Danton Affair, a 1930s play that Wajda directed on stage in 1975, this boisterous and lavish French production starring Gerard Depardieu and scripted by Jean-Claude Carriere, may have seemed like a break from contemporary Polish politics. But Depardieu’s Danton, an earthy, plain-spoken man of the people, was widely seen as a representation of Polish solidarity leader Lech Walesa, and Wojciech Pszoniak’s reserved, cerebral Robespierre, was seen as the iron-fisted military general and Polish president Wojciech Jaruzelski. The film’s politics have been widely debated, but the movie, a rare Wajda production made outside of his own country, was a hit of the 1983 New York Film Festival and an arthouse success. Presented with support from The Ashes and Diamonds Fund for Eastern European Film and The Ada Katz Fund for Literature in Film

screenings.title: You Had to Be There
screenings.description: “AN EXUBERANT AND ESSENTIAL DOC FOR COMEDY HEADS... The comedy revolution referred to by the title of Nick Davis’s sharp and effusive documentary YOU HAD TO BE THERE: HOW THE TORONTO GODSPELL IGNITED THE COMEDY REVOLUTION... is the one that took place on television in the ’70s: the creation of Saturday Night Live and SCTV and everything that grew out of them. YOU HAD TO BE THERE makes the case that the Petri dish from which the DNA of those shows was sprung was the 1972 Toronto production of Godspell, the Jesus-and-his-followers-as-hippie-clowns musical that had rocked the world when it premiered on Broadway the year before. The Toronto production featured a young Martin Short, Eugene Levy, Andrea Martin, Dave Thomas (all Canadian), and, from across the river, Detroit’s own Gilda Radner—who was the very first performer to be cast on Saturday Night, a show created by Lorne Michaels, who was also Canadian... There’s passionate testimony from the likes of Mike Myers and Lin-Manuel Miranda, who hails the show as ‘the ’27 Yankees of comedy.’ YOU HAD TO BE THERE shows you that something was in the air up there, and that it spread like the world’s happiest virus.” – Owen Gleiberman, Variety “Director Nick Davis’ terrific return to this historic event offers a laugh-a-minute trip down memory lane that’s not merely nostalgic. It’s a valuable oral history of a defining moment in pop culture... A hugely entertaining record of Canadian cultural history worthy of time and celebration. And, in perhaps the most Canadian trait ever, it’s an American production.” – Pat Mullen, POV Magazine

screenings.description: ABOUT THE DOWNTOWN FESTIVAL: The Downtown Festival is a multidisciplinary celebration of independent film, music, art, and culture held across Lower Manhattan each October. Founded and directed by filmmaker Rebekah Sherman-Myntti, the festival brings together artists across disciplines and generations through film premieres, anniversary screenings, live music performances, artist talks, and special one-night-only events. Programming is led by Sherman-Myntti and Associate Director Briana Bursten, with a focus on discovery, experimentation, community, and genuine artist-to-artist exchange. The festival’s film program runs October 9-18 at Roxy Cinema, with additional programming and special events taking place all over downtown.

screenings.title: The Wedding
screenings.description: Wesele Poland, 1972 Directed by Andrzej Wajda Starring Daniel Olbrychski, Ewa Ziętek, Marek Walczewski, Izabella Olszewska, Approx. 106 mins. The turn-of-the-century wedding between a famed poet and a peasant woman inspired the popular 1901 play The Wedding by Stanislaw Wyspiański. Written at a time when Polish intellectuals were trying to find connections with the country’s peasantry, the play is a satire of this idealistic urge, and an allegory for the nation’s history, making it ideal source material for this rarely screened adaptation. A kaleidoscopic whirl of activity, the film follows the revelries of the wedding guests, and things get more surreal as the evening goes on, and figures from Polish history appear, including a king’s jester, a medieval hero, and the leader of a peasant revolt. Wajda creates a fantasmagoria; he says he wanted “a film reality in which the worlds of thoughts, feelings, and occurrences might co-exist on an equal footing; where dream and reality would imperceptibly intertwine.” Presented with support from The Ashes and Diamonds Fund for Eastern European Film and The Ada Katz Fund for Literature in Film

screenings.title: Filipiñana
screenings.description: “A masterwork—which is all the more remarkable given that it’s the first feature by the Filipino director Rafael Manuel... The film performs a scalpel-sharp dissection of the [luxury tourism] industry, laying bare a mad microcosm of power relations—political, sexual, economic, familial, cultural, even linguistic—and the aesthetic of dominance that the resort, in Manuel’s discerning view, projects... Manuel’s approach to narrative is as original as his sense of cinematic form, and his gift for documentary-style observation is balanced by a refined sense of style.” – Richard Brody, The New Yorker “Darkly comic, visually inventive... cinematically builds into a scathing account of inequality, showing how women like Isabel are condemned to work in a place whose atmosphere is closer to that of a colonial plantation than a cushy country club.” – Jordan Mintzer, The Hollywood Reporter “An invigorating dose of arch formalism in a sea of mainstream sincerity, this is the kind of movie that asks for the viewer’s attention and patience—not because it is slow or oblique but because it’s built entirely out of details... the angle of a golf club can evoke suspense, a piece of fruit on the ground can feel like a tragedy, and a casual glance can take your breath away.” – Bilge Ebiri, Vulture “Manuel uses his fastidiously arranged tableaux to give a tension and dark sense of humor to his fiery vision of Filipino high society. Set in an eerily well-manicured golf course outside Manila, this deadpan drama, with the symmetrical style of a Wes Anderson movie, patiently snakes its way through the club’s inner workings.” – Beatrice Loayza, The New York Times ★★★★ “Brilliantly biting... In a year of several standout debuts, Manuel’s ranks among the most impressive. The microcosm he meticulously constructs makes for a rivetingly caustic indictment of his homeland.” – Carlos Aguilar, RogerEbert.com

screenings.title: The Age of Innocence
screenings.description: One breathtaking composition follows another in Scorsese’s adaptation of Edith Wharton’s Pulitzer Prize–winning masterpiece about social mores (and taboos) amongst New York’s viperous moneyed classes in late 19th-century New York, brought to life by an all-star lineup of craftspeople including cinematographer Michael Ballhaus, editor Thelma Schoonmaker, production designer Dante Ferretti, and composer Elmer Bernstein. In front of the camera there are Daniel Day-Lewis and Michelle Pfeiffer suffering beautifully as wealthy lawyer Newland Archer and Countess Ellen Olenska, the divorced pariah whom he yearns for, and Winona Ryder as Archer’s fiancée and, eventually, wife—outwardly a winsome innocent, but a cunning, cutthroat strategist where affairs of the heart are concerned. It was, Ryder stated during a recent appearance on (of all things) Hot Ones, “The role of a lifetime.”

screenings.title: Socrates
screenings.description: Beginning in the mid-’60s and ending with his death in 1977, Rossellini committed himself to producing a series of films, telefilms, and serial works that would together constitute a narrative of human progress and the history of ideas from aleolithic to present times. Socrates, initiating a tetralogy of works on epoch-defining thinkers, sets its scene in an Athens humbled by Sparta and increasingly irritated by the prickly, prodding philosopher in their midst, finally determined to silence him. Using out-of-vogue in-camera effects to transform an ancient Spanish village into Athens, probing scenes with his customized, remote-controlled Pancinor zoom, and employing a dirge-like electronic score by Mario Nascimbene, Rossellini gives us a singular vision of antiquity, one that’s downright avant-garde.

screenings.title: Lotna
screenings.description: Poland, 1959 Directed by Andrzej Wajda Starring Jerzy Pichelski, Adam Pawlikowski, Bożena Kurowska, Jerzy Moes, Mieczysław Łoza, Roman Polański Approx. 90 mins. Perhaps the most personally meaningful of Wajda’s World War II movies, LOTNA was likely inspired by the director’s admiration for his father, a Polish cavalry officer who was killed during the Katyń massacre in 1940. LOTNA is a beautiful white horse, given as a gift by a wealthy landowner to a Polish cavalry troop in the fateful year of 1939. As the Germans attack with planes and tanks, the underequipped Polish army relies on archaic resources, such as the cavalry. Symbolic and at times surreal, the film was controversial at the time of its release for suggesting Polish foolhardiness in the face of the Nazi threat. Presented with support from The Ashes and Diamonds Fund for Eastern European Film

screenings.title: Fjord
screenings.description: From two-time Palme d’Or winner Cristian Mungiu, a Norwegian woman and her devout Romanian husband relocate with their five children to a remote, close-knit, coastal town. Their teenage children form a fast bond with a neighboring family as unease begins to simmer around their rigid beliefs. When allegations of abuse emerge, they are forced to confront a system of judgment that blurs the line between concern and prejudice.

screenings.title: You Had to Be There
screenings.description: “AN EXUBERANT AND ESSENTIAL DOC FOR COMEDY HEADS... The comedy revolution referred to by the title of Nick Davis’s sharp and effusive documentary YOU HAD TO BE THERE: HOW THE TORONTO GODSPELL IGNITED THE COMEDY REVOLUTION... is the one that took place on television in the ’70s: the creation of Saturday Night Live and SCTV and everything that grew out of them. YOU HAD TO BE THERE makes the case that the Petri dish from which the DNA of those shows was sprung was the 1972 Toronto production of Godspell, the Jesus-and-his-followers-as-hippie-clowns musical that had rocked the world when it premiered on Broadway the year before. The Toronto production featured a young Martin Short, Eugene Levy, Andrea Martin, Dave Thomas (all Canadian), and, from across the river, Detroit’s own Gilda Radner—who was the very first performer to be cast on Saturday Night, a show created by Lorne Michaels, who was also Canadian... There’s passionate testimony from the likes of Mike Myers and Lin-Manuel Miranda, who hails the show as ‘the ’27 Yankees of comedy.’ YOU HAD TO BE THERE shows you that something was in the air up there, and that it spread like the world’s happiest virus.” – Owen Gleiberman, Variety “Director Nick Davis’ terrific return to this historic event offers a laugh-a-minute trip down memory lane that’s not merely nostalgic. It’s a valuable oral history of a defining moment in pop culture... A hugely entertaining record of Canadian cultural history worthy of time and celebration. And, in perhaps the most Canadian trait ever, it’s an American production.” – Pat Mullen, POV Magazine

screenings.description: Seeking a fresh start, chef Xu Fu travels to the Middle East to support his family and repay his debts. Alongside restaurant manager Ma Junsheng, he transforms the struggling Dragon Restaurant into a thriving business. But when war engulfs the city, their hard-won success is shattered and the restaurant becomes a refuge for those caught in the conflict. As danger closes in, Xu Fu must risk everything to protect his newfound community and preserve a small beacon of hope amid the devastation.

screenings.title: The Scout
screenings.description: Director González-Nasser spent six years working as a location scout. In this luminous directorial debut, she brings us into a day in the life of a young scout tasked with finding the perfect interiors for a television pilot. Sofía (Mimi Davila) moves in and out of other people’s intimate spaces and quotidian lives, tweaking her personality just enough to connect while struggling to find balance between her professional and personal worlds. With a mounting stack of parking tickets and the impertinent commentaries of her crew, she faces a series of small-yet-paralyzing obstacles that render her day increasingly exhausting. Through a constellation of quiet but poignant vignettes, the film offers an original view into the invisible labor of TV production, unfolding as an alternative symphony of a New York grappling with gentrification and a growing erosion of empathy. Presented with support from The Endowed Fund for Emerging Filmmakers 2025 89 MIN. screenings.title: Behemoth!
screenings.description: Dir. Tony Gilroy. 2026, 124 mins. U.S. DCP. Pedro Pascal gives the performance of his career so far as Alex, a cellist picking up the pieces of a fractured life, in this American drama of uncommon intelligence, humor, and grace from Academy Award–nominated writer-director Tony Gilroy (Michael Clayton). A former child prodigy living in the shadow of a storied musical family, Alex has left his position with an orchestra in Chicago—fleeing a soured relationship with a manic ex (Olivia Wilde)—and returned to Los Angeles to record Hollywood film scores and resolve unfinished family business. Using a deft flashback structure to weave in and out of his adult life, while cleverly employing a panoply of original movie compositions to both accompany and comment upon them (in a soundtrack featuring nine of the industry’s leading musicians), Gilroy turns Alex’s desire for stability, meaning, and redemption into a sophisticated drama of the highest order. Behemoth! is a thundering, savvy tribute to the power of music that builds to an emotional wallop of a climax, also featuring stellar supporting work from Eva Victor, Alexa Swinton, Kaya Ralls, Erik Griffin, JoBeth Williams, and Margarita Levieva, with Hank Azaria and Will Arnett. screenings.title: Vacances
screenings.description: FILMMAKER IN PERSON!A strange and unusual mixture of warts-and-all family portraiture, subtle exposé of class and privilege, and minimalist depiction of a particular setting that’s rendered with an almost miraculously tactile sense of presence, photographer and filmmaker Victoria Hely-Hutchinson’s VACANCES is a deceptively unassuming film. Filmed over the course of a decade at the property in Provence inhabited by Hely-Hutchinson’s outrageously uninhibited grandmother, a bohemian Austro-Hungarian countess and family matriarch, VACANCES grew out of Hely-Hutchinson’s 2016 short film of the same name, and is something of a filmic complement to her autobiographical 2023 book, “I Left My Grandmother’s House”. The documentary delves, with a grace and open-endedness that belies its analytical bite, into both the bigger-than-life personality of “granny” as well as the sometimes strained dynamics among the rest of the family, including Hely-Hutchinson’s grandfather, mother, and siblings. Unique in suggesting by turns cinema vérité, reality TV, chamber theater, and the minimalism of landscape cinema, VACANCES is a profoundly singular work – a film whose technique is nearly invisible, but which sneaks up on you with its trenchant perceptions, layered meanings, and emotional and filmic complexity.“This time-lapse film, shot over a period of ten years, follows members of several generations of a wealthy aristocratic family with Austro-Hungarian roots. The entire film is set in a Provençal villa, whose social heart is the swimming pool, around which the women gather to exchange various observations and, surreptitiously, gossip. The center of the family is the aging matriarch, who likes to talk about her extravagant, promiscuous life, but at the same time commands all the attention and authority of those around her. However, her influence gradually weakens with each passing generation.” –JI.HLAVA INTERNATIONAL DOCUMENTARY FILM FESTIVAL

A time capsule of ’80s NYC—particularly Chinatown—and a perfectly delightful blend of odd-couple romance and amiable comedy from Cheung and longtime collaborator Alex Law, who took home Best Screenplay honors at the 7th Hong Kong Film Awards for his work here. (Lowell Lo’s heartstring-tugging score was, alas, robbed.)

screenings.title: Unzipped
screenings.description: U.S., 1995 Directed by Douglas Keeve Starring Isaac Mizrahi, Linda Evangelista, Naomi Campbell, Cindy Crawford, Kate Moss Executive Producer Nina Santisi Approx. 73 min. “Isaac Mizrahi as he conceived and contorted the way through to his fall 1994 show, [dashing] around a deserted SoHo with pal Sandra Bernhard; [meeting] with Naomi Campbell, Linda Evangelista, and baby Kate Moss for fittings; and [racing] uptown to an audience with Eartha Kitt... Hair-raising deadlines, delirious Bette Davis impressions, and the hostile but exhilarating act of executing a designer’s vision come together in a work that set the bar for all fashion films after.” – Vogue

screenings.title: Smart Girl (w/q&a)
screenings.description: In an attempt to one-up her smart sister, Hannah Lynn Crane copies her by writing a book. When she finds out her friend Barbara from Scrabble Group used to write romance novels, she enlists her help. Together they start brainstorming a daring age-gap romance novel, but when Barbara mysteriously disappears right before tackling the sex scenes, Hannah is left to her own devices. She falls down a dangerously addictive, GILF-riddled path to learn what being smart actually means.

screenings.title: Bread Day preceded by The Train Stop
screenings.description: “In Loznitsa’s The Train Stop, in the middle of the night, the train doesn’t arrive. The waiting room is full of heavy sleepers, some folded over on their laps, some splayed out over the benches. What could rouse them? Maybe the answer is not a train, but a film. Consider Dvortsevoy’s similarly existential Bread Day. Sure, the rickety cart carrying the week’s delivery of bread to Township 3 of Zhikharevo barely seems to count as a train. It’s manually pushed by the pensioners who will soon argue strenuously with each other as they divvy up its contents. But their shouting is so vigorous, their insults so inventive, that questions of categorization quickly dissipate as the elderly residents, their goats in tow, battle to have the last word.” —Series curator Genevieve Yue

screenings.title: Korczak
screenings.description: Poland, 1990 Directed by Andrzej Wajda Screenplay by Agnieszka Holland Starring Wojciech Pszoniak, Ewa Dałkowska, Teresa Budzisz-Krzyżanowska, Marzena Trybała Approx. 118 mins. Janusz Korczak was a renowned doctor, teacher, and author who ran a Jewish orphanage in the Warsaw Ghetto, and ultimately sacrificed his life to stay with them until his deportation to Treblinka. With a bracingly unsentimental script by Agnieszka Holland, and stunning black-and-white cinematography by Robby Müller intercut with actual archival footage, Wajda recreates life in the ghetto in vivid detail. Wajda fought for years to get this film made, claiming “Jewish themes in Polish culture have been virtually banned for twenty years.” Presented with support from The Ashes and Diamonds Fund for Eastern European Film and The Joan S. Constantiner Fund for Jewish and Holocaust Films, donated by Leon Constantiner and Family

screenings.title: Filipiñana
screenings.description: “A masterwork—which is all the more remarkable given that it’s the first feature by the Filipino director Rafael Manuel... The film performs a scalpel-sharp dissection of the [luxury tourism] industry, laying bare a mad microcosm of power relations—political, sexual, economic, familial, cultural, even linguistic—and the aesthetic of dominance that the resort, in Manuel’s discerning view, projects... Manuel’s approach to narrative is as original as his sense of cinematic form, and his gift for documentary-style observation is balanced by a refined sense of style.” – Richard Brody, The New Yorker “Darkly comic, visually inventive... cinematically builds into a scathing account of inequality, showing how women like Isabel are condemned to work in a place whose atmosphere is closer to that of a colonial plantation than a cushy country club.” – Jordan Mintzer, The Hollywood Reporter “An invigorating dose of arch formalism in a sea of mainstream sincerity, this is the kind of movie that asks for the viewer’s attention and patience—not because it is slow or oblique but because it’s built entirely out of details... the angle of a golf club can evoke suspense, a piece of fruit on the ground can feel like a tragedy, and a casual glance can take your breath away.” – Bilge Ebiri, Vulture “Manuel uses his fastidiously arranged tableaux to give a tension and dark sense of humor to his fiery vision of Filipino high society. Set in an eerily well-manicured golf course outside Manila, this deadpan drama, with the symmetrical style of a Wes Anderson movie, patiently snakes its way through the club’s inner workings.” – Beatrice Loayza, The New York Times ★★★★ “Brilliantly biting... In a year of several standout debuts, Manuel’s ranks among the most impressive. The microcosm he meticulously constructs makes for a rivetingly caustic indictment of his homeland.” – Carlos Aguilar, RogerEbert.com

screenings.title: The Only Living Pickpocket in New York
screenings.description: Dir. Noah Segan. 2026, 88 mins. U.S. DCP. In a star turn of effortless command and charisma, John Turturro plays Harry, an aging petty thief from the Bronx who knows his professional days are numbered: the tactile craft of the pickpocket has become increasingly irrelevant in a digital world. Yet he must still make ends meet, especially in caring for his severely disabled wife. When Harry swipes the wallet of an ill-chosen mark (Will Price), however, he is thrust into a borough-hopping race against time to put things back in their right place. Building to a poignant climax, writer-director Noah Segan’s elegant love letter to both New York and to bygone cinematic eras recalls both the 1970s, with its grungy urban antiheroes, and the 1990s, in its American indie ethos. In addition to being a peak of Turturro’s illustrious career, the film features a terrific cast including Steve Buscemi, Giancarlo Esposito, Tatiana Maslany, Victoria Moroles, and Kelvin Han Yee. A Sony Pictures Classics release. Tickets: $35 / discounted for MoMI and NYFF members ($30). There is a $1.50 transaction fee per ticket for all online purchases. screenings.title: The Adventures of Prince Achmed: 100th anniversary screening with live musical accompaniment
screenings.description: 35mm with live piano accompaniment by Charlie Judkins Introduced by Whitney Grace, author of Lotte Reiniger: Pioneer of Film Animation Dir. Lotte Reiniger. 1926, 80 mins. Germany. 35mm. Eleven years before Disney’s Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs, Lotte Reiniger’s stop-motion feature The Adventures of Prince Achmed, debuted in 1926 at the Volksbühne in Berlin, during the height of the Weimar Republic. Adapted from the tales known as the Arabian Nights, the film follows the adventures of a young prince atop a magical, flying horse who joins forces with the likes of Aladdin and a fabled witch. To evade his destined ill fate, he saves a beautiful princess and battles a sorcerer’s army of monsters. This thrilling, sensuous tale, told through Reiniger’s meticulous cut-paper silhouette animation technique, still enthralls audiences of all ages one hundred years later. Featuring live musical accompaniment by Charlie Judkins and preceded by a lecture by Whitney Grace, author of Lotte Reiniger: Pioneer of Film Animation. Special Guests: Whitney Grace is a professional writer, researcher, appraiser, and pop culture historian. Her books include Lotte Reiniger: Pioneer of Film Animation and her fantasy/horror novel Iron Impetigo. She hosts the Toon-In Talk Podcast and is pursuing a gemology degree at GIA. Charlie Judkins is an internationally recognized pianist specializing in Traditional Jazz, Blues & Ragtime piano styles. screenings.title: Trains, Children & Dreams: A Shorts Program
screenings.description: “The train that begins Bruce Conner’s Valse Triste also sets in motion a child’s dreaming. Like Conner’s synechdocal found footage classic A Movie, the loosely connected scenes that follow are retrieved from film history, as if to say that our dreams are made of movies, or vice versa. Wasn’t it a kind of dream to imagine, in 1896, that the Lumières’ train would tumble into the audience? Or that, in Ignacio Agüero’s One Hundred Children Waiting for the Train, the children of Lo Hermida, a working class neighborhood on the outskirts of Santiago, might one day see themselves on a real cinema screen? Or, despite the protest made by one of Harun Farocki’s young daughters—‘I don’t want to hear or see any more trains!’—the locomotive that arrives just as she and her sister drift off to sleep?” —Series curator Genevieve Yue

screenings.description: Marion Cotillard has one of her greatest roles as Ewa, a Polish Catholic immigrant newly arrived in Ellis Island, trying to find the means to free her sister from quarantine in a c. 1921 New York City that’s full of lures and snares, among them Joaquin Phoenix’s smalltime pimp and tinhorn impresario and Jeremy Renner’s Bowery illusionist. A richly textured film of disarming depths of feeling from Gray, whose beguiling closing shot resonates long after the credits roll. “We effectively destroyed the film negative with various techniques,” said Darius Khondji, “to achieve the desired emotional aesthetic of that era.”

screenings.title: In the Mouth of Madness
screenings.description: Dir. John Carpenter. 1994, 95 mins. U.S. 35mm. With Sam Neill, Jürgen Prochnow, Julie Carmen, David Warner, John Glover, Charlton Heston. John Carpenter’s metacinematic tribute to the nightmarish underworlds of H. P. Lovecraft stars Sam Neill as a John Trent, a mild-mannered insurance investigator who gradually descends into hysteria while seeking the whereabouts Sutter Cane, a Lovecraft-esque cult writer who has gone missing. Upon arriving in a small New England town, Trent begins to realize that he may be caught within one of Cane’s stories, which only grows more nightmarish and sinister as he encounters surreal phenomena. The practical creature effects recall Lovecraft’s imagery while maintaining a sense of sly Carpenter humor that skirts the absurd. Aptly, a significant cult following has grown around In the Mouth of Madness in the decades since its release, and Neill’s unfettered portrayal of insanity has much to do with its beloved horror status. screenings.title: The Illiac Passion
screenings.description: Markopoulos corralled together the underground’s haute monde—Taylor Mead, Gerard Malanga, Jack Smith, Gregory Battcock and, in the role of Poseidon, Andy Warhol—for his radical reinterpretation of Aeschylus’s Prometheus Bound, in which the filmmaker can be heard on the soundtrack reciting Thoreau’s translation of the source text betwixt snatches of Bartók’s Cantata Profana. A rebel posing a direct challenge to Zeus’s absolute authority, Prometheus was a figure of fascination for Markopoulos, who saw in the outlaw Titan something of a kindred spirit. Hence his vainglorious description of The Illiac Passion: “Metamorphosis of the filmmaker. Passions of the filmmaker. Out of his breast the free flowing blood of the creation of a motion picture which depicts the passions of mankind and of everyman in general.”

screenings.title: Vacances
screenings.description: FILMMAKER IN PERSON!A strange and unusual mixture of warts-and-all family portraiture, subtle exposé of class and privilege, and minimalist depiction of a particular setting that’s rendered with an almost miraculously tactile sense of presence, photographer and filmmaker Victoria Hely-Hutchinson’s VACANCES is a deceptively unassuming film. Filmed over the course of a decade at the property in Provence inhabited by Hely-Hutchinson’s outrageously uninhibited grandmother, a bohemian Austro-Hungarian countess and family matriarch, VACANCES grew out of Hely-Hutchinson’s 2016 short film of the same name, and is something of a filmic complement to her autobiographical 2023 book, “I Left My Grandmother’s House”. The documentary delves, with a grace and open-endedness that belies its analytical bite, into both the bigger-than-life personality of “granny” as well as the sometimes strained dynamics among the rest of the family, including Hely-Hutchinson’s grandfather, mother, and siblings. Unique in suggesting by turns cinema vérité, reality TV, chamber theater, and the minimalism of landscape cinema, VACANCES is a profoundly singular work – a film whose technique is nearly invisible, but which sneaks up on you with its trenchant perceptions, layered meanings, and emotional and filmic complexity.“This time-lapse film, shot over a period of ten years, follows members of several generations of a wealthy aristocratic family with Austro-Hungarian roots. The entire film is set in a Provençal villa, whose social heart is the swimming pool, around which the women gather to exchange various observations and, surreptitiously, gossip. The center of the family is the aging matriarch, who likes to talk about her extravagant, promiscuous life, but at the same time commands all the attention and authority of those around her. However, her influence gradually weakens with each passing generation.” –JI.HLAVA INTERNATIONAL DOCUMENTARY FILM FESTIVAL

What follows includes JFK assassination trauma, a pregnancy scare, mother-daughter sexual competition, and one miraculous rescue, with devastating dynamic duo Cher and Ryder pushing one another to histrionic heights.

screenings.title: Earth
screenings.description: Dovzhenko’s final silent feature, which depicts a clash between reactionary landowning peasants and modernizing paupers bringing the first tractor to their corner of the Ukrainian countryside, has by now spawned nearly a century of debate: is it a propagandist paean to the collectivization project in Stalin’s first Five-Year Plan, which would have catastrophic results in the Ukrainian Famine of 1932-33, or, as certain Soviet censors suspected, an on-the-sly celebration of a Ukrainian folk culture grounded in an ancient connection between the peasants and the soil they’ve so long tilled, threatened with impending erasure? What is not up for question is that Earth is among the greatest of films from the silent film canon, its distinct synthesis of Eisenstein, Pudovkin, and Vertov making it something like a summation of what had come before it, while its lyric ode to the natural world and those that live with it in harmony blazes a trail for the Ukrainian Poetic Cinema of the future to follow.

screenings.title: Playing with Fire: an Ecosexual Emergency
screenings.description: Following their two previous films – GOODBYE GAULEY MOUNTAIN: AN ECOSEXUAL LOVE STORY (2014) and WATER MAKES US WET: AN ECOSEXUAL ADVENTURE (2019) – Annie Sprinkle and Beth Stephens bring us the third chapter in their climate crisis trilogy: PLAYING WITH FIRE: AN ECOSEXUAL EMERGENCY. With the climate crisis worsening with each passing season, the artist/activist duo sound the alarm by enlisting a collective of artists, elders, witches, neighbors, and friends, to examine the ways we can support the health of our dear Earth. Partially narrated by Boulder Creek’s mythical white peacock Albert and culminating in a ceremonial Wedding to Fire in the Redwoods, PLAYING WITH FIRE is a powerful portrait of queer resilience but also a reckoning with the power of fire, with its capacity to heal and its potential to destroy.Co-sponsored by Climate Film Festival and Queer New York International Arts Festival.Annie Sprinkle & Beth Stephens will be here in person for both screenings, and will present a ten-minute performative introduction before each show, “Ecosex 101”!On Saturday, Sprinkle & Stephens will appear for a post-screening discussion and Q&A led by Barbara Carellas, author of “The Book of Ecstasy”, and on Sunday, Angelo Madsen (director of A BODY TO LIVE IN) will lead a Q&A. Viewers are encouraged to dress up in the themes of fire and ecosex.After the Saturday screening, all are welcome to join a reception in the lobby. Beth and Annie will honor two legends of golden age adult entertainment and the co-founders of the first pornstar support group, Club 90. Veronica Vera is turning 80 and Veronica Hart is turning 70. Birthday cake will be served, and signed books and merch will be available for purchase.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.description: One breathtaking composition follows another in Scorsese’s adaptation of Edith Wharton’s Pulitzer Prize–winning masterpiece about social mores (and taboos) amongst New York’s viperous moneyed classes in late 19th-century New York, brought to life by an all-star lineup of craftspeople including cinematographer Michael Ballhaus, editor Thelma Schoonmaker, production designer Dante Ferretti, and composer Elmer Bernstein. In front of the camera there are Daniel Day-Lewis and Michelle Pfeiffer suffering beautifully as wealthy lawyer Newland Archer and Countess Ellen Olenska, the divorced pariah whom he yearns for, and Winona Ryder as Archer’s fiancée and, eventually, wife—outwardly a winsome innocent, but a cunning, cutthroat strategist where affairs of the heart are concerned. It was, Ryder stated during a recent appearance on (of all things) Hot Ones, “The role of a lifetime.”

screenings.description: No one wields a ’Scope frame with quite the same flexibility and dynamism as Hark, and the spectacular, Sergio Leone–inspired Once Upon a Time in China—perhaps the crucial film of the 1990s wuxia revival—shows Hark at his most flamboyant, keeping up with the human whirlwind that is Jet Li, here in the role of physician, martial artist, and 19th-century Cantonese folk hero Wong Fei-hung, who’s pitted against unscrupulous gangsters, human traffickers from the West, and his inconvenient feelings for “13th Aunt” Rosamund Kwan. Showstopping set pieces come fast and furious en route to a shoot-the-works shipboard finale; a monumental work of kinetic cinema.

Hoberman called Southland Tales “a visionary film about the end of times. There hasn’t been anything comparable in American movies since Mulholland Drive.” Manic, messy, and endlessly referential, Southland Tales skewers George W. Bush, reality TV, and digital media to present an unforgettable satire of post-9/11 America. The film was not—and still may not be for everyone—but what it lacks in precision it more than makes up for in ambition. The film is set in the aftermath of two catastrophic nuclear attacks in Texas and follows the intertwining storylines of an action film actor, a porn star, and a pair of twin brothers. screenings.description: Brecht’s adaptation of Sophocles’s Antigone—concerning the title character’s rebellion against the uncle, King Creon, who has condemned her to death—is performed in its entirety in Straub and Huillet’s final film set in the ancient world, which recalls their 1975 Moses und Aron in its antiquarian setting: the ruins of a Greek theatre in Segesta, Sicily.

screenings.title: Once Upon a Time in China II
screenings.description: No one wields a ’Scope frame with quite the same flexibility and dynamism as Hark, and the spectacular, Sergio Leone–inspired Once Upon a Time in China II shows Hark at his most inspired, keeping up with the human whirlwind that is Jet Li, here returning to the role of physician, martial artist, and 19th-century Cantonese folk hero Wong Fei-hung. Traveling to Canton for a medical conference, Wong finds a city in chaos, with the anti-western White Lotus Cult seeking to snuff out foreign influence by any means necessary, and government forces—including officer Donnie Yen—resorting to violent measures against Dr. Sun Yat-sen’s republican revolutionaries. Unrelenting, utterly dazzling, pedal-to-the-metal action cinema.

screenings.title: Playing with Fire: an Ecosexual Emergency
screenings.description: Following their two previous films – GOODBYE GAULEY MOUNTAIN: AN ECOSEXUAL LOVE STORY (2014) and WATER MAKES US WET: AN ECOSEXUAL ADVENTURE (2019) – Annie Sprinkle and Beth Stephens bring us the third chapter in their climate crisis trilogy: PLAYING WITH FIRE: AN ECOSEXUAL EMERGENCY. With the climate crisis worsening with each passing season, the artist/activist duo sound the alarm by enlisting a collective of artists, elders, witches, neighbors, and friends, to examine the ways we can support the health of our dear Earth. Partially narrated by Boulder Creek’s mythical white peacock Albert and culminating in a ceremonial Wedding to Fire in the Redwoods, PLAYING WITH FIRE is a powerful portrait of queer resilience but also a reckoning with the power of fire, with its capacity to heal and its potential to destroy.Co-sponsored by Climate Film Festival and Queer New York International Arts Festival.Annie Sprinkle & Beth Stephens will be here in person for both screenings, and will present a ten-minute performative introduction before each show, “Ecosex 101”!On Saturday, Sprinkle & Stephens will appear for a post-screening discussion and Q&A led by Barbara Carellas, author of “The Book of Ecstasy”, and on Sunday, Angelo Madsen (director of A BODY TO LIVE IN) will lead a Q&A. Viewers are encouraged to dress up in the themes of fire and ecosex.After the Saturday screening, all are welcome to join a reception in the lobby. Beth and Annie will honor two legends of golden age adult entertainment and the co-founders of the first pornstar support group, Club 90. Veronica Vera is turning 80 and Veronica Hart is turning 70. Birthday cake will be served, and signed books and merch will be available for purchase.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.description: Dir. Michael Powell. 1960, 101 mins. 4K DCP. With Karlheinz Böhm, Anna Massey, Moira Shearer. J. Hoberman writes,” A great film maudit can derail or even terminate a career. Michael Powell never recovered from the scandal of Peeping Tom.” Initially reviled, but now considered a classic study of cinematic voyeurism, Powell’s 1960 masterpiece concerns a young photographer obsessed with killing women and filming their final contorted expressions. Martin Scorsese has described it is a film that “says everything that can be said about filmmaking, [and] the process of dealing with film.” Tickets: $17.50 / $12 senior and students / $10 youth / $7 MoMI members. screenings.title: Once Upon a Time in China III
screenings.description: In Jet Li’s third outing as the legendary Wong Fei-hung, master of both inflicting pain and relieving it, Wong and Rosamund Kwan’s “13th Aunt” travel from Foshan to Beijing to meet with his father, there finding preparations underway for a colorful competition to crown a “Lion Dance King” and learning of a plot to assassinate statesman and court favorite Li Hongzhang. With leadership at home slipping into self-involved venality and foreign powers licking their chops at the prospect of dividing China up amongst themselves, Wong will have to hold the line one more time—and as one has come to expect of the series, the results are nothing short of spectacular.

screenings.title: Arsenal
screenings.description: The film that made Dovzhenko’s international reputation, Arsenal depicts—in thrillingly innovative, lyric cinematic language—a 1918 episode in the Russian Civil War, a worker’s uprising at Kyiv’s Arsenal Factory, and its brutal military suppression, in the midst of fighting between Bolshevik forces and the Central Rada of the Ukrainian People’s Republic, in whose ranks Dovzhenko may have served for a time. One of a quartet of films commissioned by Soviet authorities to celebrate the 10th anniversary of the October Revolution and, of the four, the most ambivalent, showing an understanding, in turns, of both the universalist, workers-of-the-world-unite Bolshevik cause and a Ukrainian nationalism rooted in soul and soil.

screenings.title: Vacances
screenings.description: FILMMAKER IN PERSON!A strange and unusual mixture of warts-and-all family portraiture, subtle exposé of class and privilege, and minimalist depiction of a particular setting that’s rendered with an almost miraculously tactile sense of presence, photographer and filmmaker Victoria Hely-Hutchinson’s VACANCES is a deceptively unassuming film. Filmed over the course of a decade at the property in Provence inhabited by Hely-Hutchinson’s outrageously uninhibited grandmother, a bohemian Austro-Hungarian countess and family matriarch, VACANCES grew out of Hely-Hutchinson’s 2016 short film of the same name, and is something of a filmic complement to her autobiographical 2023 book, “I Left My Grandmother’s House”. The documentary delves, with a grace and open-endedness that belies its analytical bite, into both the bigger-than-life personality of “granny” as well as the sometimes strained dynamics among the rest of the family, including Hely-Hutchinson’s grandfather, mother, and siblings. Unique in suggesting by turns cinema vérité, reality TV, chamber theater, and the minimalism of landscape cinema, VACANCES is a profoundly singular work – a film whose technique is nearly invisible, but which sneaks up on you with its trenchant perceptions, layered meanings, and emotional and filmic complexity.“This time-lapse film, shot over a period of ten years, follows members of several generations of a wealthy aristocratic family with Austro-Hungarian roots. The entire film is set in a Provençal villa, whose social heart is the swimming pool, around which the women gather to exchange various observations and, surreptitiously, gossip. The center of the family is the aging matriarch, who likes to talk about her extravagant, promiscuous life, but at the same time commands all the attention and authority of those around her. However, her influence gradually weakens with each passing generation.” –JI.HLAVA INTERNATIONAL DOCUMENTARY FILM FESTIVAL

screenings.title: Shchors
screenings.description: A biopic of the “Red Commander of the Ukraine,” Bolshevik commander Mykola Shchors, starring Yevgeny Samoylov in the title role, Shchors was personally commissioned by Joseph Stalin himself, and its production was a fraught one for Dovzhenko, whose health suffered grievously from the make-or-break pressure he faced to toe the line. The eventual results pleased the General Secretary—Dovzhenko would be awarded his first of two Stalin Prizes in 1941—though the film endures less for its vigorous, saber-rattling hagiography than the moments of ineffable poetry with which it’s embroidered, rooted as always in a deep sense of Ukrainian cultural tradition and relish in the natural world. “As in all [Dovzhenko’s] best work, Shchors leaves in the memory burning images of death and of passionate life” —Jay Leyda

screenings.title: The Terminator
screenings.description: Too many sequels and an incalculable cultural impact later, it’s sometimes forgotten what a hot and nasty little movie Cameron’s original Terminator was, dropping peak-physique Schwarzenegger into a sleazy Los Angeles of leather bars, punk rockers, and skid rows, where he quickly proceeds to killing cops by the score and tracking down mother-to-be of humankind’s savior Linda Hamilton. Working for the very last time with budget constraints, Cameron—and FX gurus Stan Winston and Gene Warren Jr.—deliver the goods and how, in a grimy lil’ chef d’oeuvre that gave us Cyberdine, Skynet, and a whole lexicon for discussing extinction-level singularity events.

screenings.title: The Downtown Festival: Slauson Rec + Q&A
screenings.description: Slauson Rec examines the fine line between mentorship and manipulation in the pursuit of making art within an experimental theater collective. In 2018, Shia LaBeouf launched a free theater school at the Slauson Rec Center in South Central, Los Angeles. What started as an open, egalitarian workshop quickly evolved into intense daily rehearsals led by Shia, pushing participants to their limits. First-time filmmaker Leo Lewis O’Neil, a participant from day one, documents this complex journey of shifting power dynamics, and the lasting impact on the diverse group over three years.

screenings.title: Vacances
screenings.description: FILMMAKER IN PERSON!A strange and unusual mixture of warts-and-all family portraiture, subtle exposé of class and privilege, and minimalist depiction of a particular setting that’s rendered with an almost miraculously tactile sense of presence, photographer and filmmaker Victoria Hely-Hutchinson’s VACANCES is a deceptively unassuming film. Filmed over the course of a decade at the property in Provence inhabited by Hely-Hutchinson’s outrageously uninhibited grandmother, a bohemian Austro-Hungarian countess and family matriarch, VACANCES grew out of Hely-Hutchinson’s 2016 short film of the same name, and is something of a filmic complement to her autobiographical 2023 book, “I Left My Grandmother’s House”. The documentary delves, with a grace and open-endedness that belies its analytical bite, into both the bigger-than-life personality of “granny” as well as the sometimes strained dynamics among the rest of the family, including Hely-Hutchinson’s grandfather, mother, and siblings. Unique in suggesting by turns cinema vérité, reality TV, chamber theater, and the minimalism of landscape cinema, VACANCES is a profoundly singular work – a film whose technique is nearly invisible, but which sneaks up on you with its trenchant perceptions, layered meanings, and emotional and filmic complexity.“This time-lapse film, shot over a period of ten years, follows members of several generations of a wealthy aristocratic family with Austro-Hungarian roots. The entire film is set in a Provençal villa, whose social heart is the swimming pool, around which the women gather to exchange various observations and, surreptitiously, gossip. The center of the family is the aging matriarch, who likes to talk about her extravagant, promiscuous life, but at the same time commands all the attention and authority of those around her. However, her influence gradually weakens with each passing generation.” –JI.HLAVA INTERNATIONAL DOCUMENTARY FILM FESTIVAL

screenings.description: Catherine lives a life of luxury, but nothing has truly brought her happiness since the death of her beloved father. Aloof and disinterested in her husband and daughter, she prefers to spend her evenings engaging in sensual fantasies up in the dark attic. But one stormy night, while seated in front of her large childhood mirror, her father—or a demon taking his appearance—appears in the reflection, promising her untold pleasures if she simply comes through the glass. Frightened at first, Catherine eventually gives in to temptation and begins to visit the world on the other side of the mirror—with each trip becoming increasingly sinister as the long-buried dark truths of her childhood begin to become more and more clear.

Trouble is, Jeffries' musings may just be the truth.

screenings.title: Rear Window
screenings.description: One of Alfred Hitchcock's very best efforts, REAR WINDOW is a crackling suspense film where the protagonist is a seemingly ordinary man who gets himself in trouble for his secret desires. Laid up with a broken leg, photojournalist L.B. Jeffries (James Stewart) is confined to his tiny apartment. To pass the time between visits from his nurse and his fashion model girlfriend (Grace Kelly), the binocular-wielding Jeffries stares through the rear window of his apartment and casually concocts a scenario in which a neighbor across the courtyard has murdered his wife. Trouble is, Jeffries' musings may just be the truth.

screenings.title: Narrow Rooms: Les Fantômes Du Hard + Fistule
screenings.description: Most kinky queers in NYC know all about the Mineshaft, the legendary, long-shuttered NYC sex club in the Meatpacking District that was in operation from 1976 to 1985. But across the Atlantic, France’s first “hard” gay BDSM sex club was also called Mineshaft, and it has remained a sacred space for BDSM and fetish sex in Marseille since its opening in 1967. In this pair of short experimental documentaries, director Lazare Lazarus and friends excavate the archive left by the Mineshaft’s founder Jean-Pierre Fouque. Chapter 1 tells the story of the squatters who took over Fouque’s apartment after his death in 2022 and discovered his archive, while illuminating aspects of the club owner’s life – his lovers, political views, activism, and more. Chapter 2, co-directed with Lupa Charon Gateff, is more of a found-footage experimental porno mixtape, using the Mineshaft’s archive of hardcore gay porn and BDSM videotapes to take us into the dungeons of Europe, both real and imagined. These two shorts will be followed by Emre Busse’s FISTULE, which invites the audience into a realm where an anal fissure serves as a dramatic springboard, exposing the absurdity of societal norms with a mix of tragedy, camp, and sexuality. If you’re a fan of the films of Liz Purchell (ASK ANY BUDDY), Ryan A. White (RAW! UNCUT! VIDEO!), and Yann Gonzalez (KNIFE + HEART), you’ll find much to enjoy in this month’s program.Lazare LazarusLES FANTÔMES DU HARD, CHAPTER 12023, 35 min, DCP. screenings.title: Okja
screenings.description: The titular beast is a gentle, lumbering, lovable “super pig” created by big agribusiness, peacefully raised in the South Korean countryside by young Mija (Ahn Seo-hyun) before being spirited off to the US, sweeping both pet and owner into a conflict between animal rights activists and mercenary corporate forces. A dark science fiction fable, its impressive ensemble cast includes Tilda Swinton, Paul Dano, and Jake Gyllenhaal. “[Okja] represents a departure toward a different type of image, a different texture and look: something very blue and metallic, with lots of compressed cityscapes and a bit of gold in the flesh tones… [Visual effects supervisor Erik de Boer] sat in with us [during the color grading] where we took every single shot of Okja in the film and treated each one individually for aspects of color and light.” —Darius Khondji

screenings.title: Strangers on a Train
screenings.description: “Criss cross.” Hitchcock’s adaptation of Highsmith’s 1951 page-turner kicks off with a casual encounter that reads like a same-sex pickup, as tennis star Guy Haines (Farley Granger) inadvertently agrees to “swap murders” with preening rich kid Bruno Anthony (Robert Walker, in a career performance), and continues through some of the finest set pieces of Hitch’s career: a tennis match at Forest Hills, Bruno stalking his prey through a vulgar county fair, and an out-of-control carousel.

screenings.title: Socrates
screenings.description: Beginning in the mid-’60s and ending with his death in 1977, Rossellini committed himself to producing a series of films, telefilms, and serial works that would together constitute a narrative of human progress and the history of ideas from aleolithic to present times. Socrates, initiating a tetralogy of works on epoch-defining thinkers, sets its scene in an Athens humbled by Sparta and increasingly irritated by the prickly, prodding philosopher in their midst, finally determined to silence him. Using out-of-vogue in-camera effects to transform an ancient Spanish village into Athens, probing scenes with his customized, remote-controlled Pancinor zoom, and employing a dirge-like electronic score by Mario Nascimbene, Rossellini gives us a singular vision of antiquity, one that’s downright avant-garde.

screenings.title: Okja
screenings.description: The titular beast is a gentle, lumbering, lovable “super pig” created by big agribusiness, peacefully raised in the South Korean countryside by young Mija (Ahn Seo-hyun) before being spirited off to the US, sweeping both pet and owner into a conflict between animal rights activists and mercenary corporate forces. A dark science fiction fable, its impressive ensemble cast includes Tilda Swinton, Paul Dano, and Jake Gyllenhaal. “[Okja] represents a departure toward a different type of image, a different texture and look: something very blue and metallic, with lots of compressed cityscapes and a bit of gold in the flesh tones… [Visual effects supervisor Erik de Boer] sat in with us [during the color grading] where we took every single shot of Okja in the film and treated each one individually for aspects of color and light.” —Darius Khondji

screenings.title: Zvenygora
screenings.description: A hunt for the Scythian treasure trove of the title, a staple of Ukrainian folklore, becomes a jumping off point for a dizzying tour of a nation’s history, traditions, and fables, fleetly flitting between paeans to nature and man-made industry, a modern present and a mythic past, materialist fact and mystical fantasy. “My most interesting picture for me. I made it in one breath—a hundred days. Unusually complicated in structure, eclectic in form, the film gave me, a self-taught production worker, the fortuitous opportunity of trying myself out in every genre. It was a catalogue of all my creative abilities.” —Oleksandr Dovzhenko

screenings.title: Fantasia
screenings.description: Walt Disney (and eleven uncredited directors). 1940, 124 mins. U.S. DCP. Disney put it all on the line for this passion project combining his love of cartoons and classical music. Though the result baffled many in its day, Fantasia went on to be one of the most beloved, influential films of all time. Set to works by Bach, Tchaikovsky, Beethoven, Stravinsky, and more, the wordless, exquisitely hand-drawn segments that make up this ambitious masterpiece constitute a high point in animation. Among the most marvelous sequences is its finale, a diptych of the profane and the sacred juxtaposing Modest Mussorgsky’s frenetic and terrifying “Night on Bald Mountain” and Franz Schubert’s ecstatic hymn “Ave Maria.” The former, set on the diabolical Walpurgis Night, is perhaps cinema’s greatest Halloween party. screenings.description: Set in the Soviet Far East in the not-too-distant future, Dovzhenko’s film takes its title from a fictitious Siberian city that, as home to a strategically vital airfield, is targeted for conquest by the duplicitous forces of the Japanese Empire. A vision of technological utopianism and natural splendor, composed with dash and dynamism by cinematographer Eduard Tissé—a regular Eisenstein collaborator—in which the forces of the Revolution must contend with samurai saboteurs, counterrevolutionary kulaks, and rabble-rousing “Old Believer” Christians, pushing Soviet civilization into the wilds of the Pacific coast. Part spy thriller, part full-throated agitprop, part pantheistic bliss-out, and pure Dovzhenko.

screenings.title: Faust
screenings.description: Dir. F. W. Murnau. 1926, 106 mins. Germany. DCP. With Emil Jannings, Gösta Ekman, Camilla Horn, William Dieterle. Having already helped revolutionize the art of cinema with the German expressionist masterworks Nosferatu and The Last Laugh, F. W. Murnau created the equally astonishing supernatural Faust, adapting the classic German legend of an alchemist who makes a pact with the devil for eternal youth. This magnificent production—Murnau’s final German film before coming to Hollywood and directing Sunrise—is one of the great accomplishments of the legendary Ufa Studios in Berlin, anchored by a diabolical Emil Jannings as Mephisto. The film’s grand designs and special effects include such unforgettable sights as flying banshees and the devil spreading his wings (and the plague) over a small town (imagery that would directly inspire the “Night on Bald Mountain” segment of Disney’s Fantasia). This new restoration of the original German version of the film (with hand-painted intertitles) features a score compiled from historic photoplay music by the Mont Alto Motion Picture Orchestra. screenings.description: An automobile driving from Madrid to Almeria becomes a veritable pressure cooker in Saura’s formally audacious road movie. The passengers are a well-to-do industrialist, Fernando (Fernando Cebrián); his wife, Teresa (Chaplin, blonde and blasé); and Fernando’s architect colleague, Antonio (Juan Luis Galiardo), who Fernando is increasingly convinced has been having an affair with Teresa. Boasting some of the most blinding whites you’ll ever see in a black-and-white film, which only adds to its oneiric quality, the little-screened Stress is Three is an achievement on par with Saura and Chaplin’s very best, a withering critique of bourgeois hedonism and Spanish machismo ripe for rediscovery.

With Anthony Quinn, Alan Bates, Lila Kedrova, Irene Papa, George Fountas, Eleni Anousaki, Sotiris Moustakas, George Vogiatzis, Anna Kyriakou. Basil (Alan Bates), an uptight young English writer of Greek ancestry, meets an older, free-spirited Greek peasant named Zorba (Anthony Quinn), who has a zeal for everything he does, on the island of Crete. While Zorba pursues a relationship with Madame Hortense (Lila Kedrova), an aging French courtesan, the inhibited Basil summons up the courage to court a young widow. The rambunctious Zorba teaches Basil how to live life to the fullest in this adaptation of Nikos Kazantzakis’s novel. This breakthrough of Greek cinema was an international sensation, winning three Oscars, including Kedrova for Best Supporting Actress, Best Cinematography, and Best Art Direction, as well as nominations for Best Picture, Best Actor, and Best Director for Cacoyannis. screenings.description: (BRONENOSETS POTEMKIN)“POTEMKIN used [Eisenstein’s] new set of rules to create what has been called the most perfect and concise example of film structure. Like STRIKE, [POTEMKIN] has no hero, only the masses, and no plot, only an incident plucked from the pre-history of the Revolution.” –Standish Lawder, EISENSTEIN AND CONSTRUCTIVISM“POTEMKIN was the first work to embody, in their most tangible form, various principles of construction peculiar to the medium: montage (or editing) and parallel action (the expansion of time through spatial manipulation); or, in sum, the purely formal deployment of objective action to create psychological dimensions. Eisenstein was not the first ‘film artist,’ but he was the first to be so pure, the first to use photography like painting in movement, photography like verbal imagery. screenings.description: Homer with a ball-peen hammer. Kidnapped and stuffed in a hole without explanation for 15 years of solitary confinement, when Oh Dae-su (Choi Min-sik) is suddenly let loose on the streets, he’s stone-cold pissed off and very, very dangerous. Winner of the Grand Prix at Cannes and an international pop phenomenon, Oldboy was a revenge thriller unlike any that had come before, featuring passages of pure bravura filmmaking (that one-shot hallway donnybrook!) and surreal sicko humor that’ll put you off of sushi for a while. “Put together with brutally uncompromising style [and] the cold-steel edge of a knife against your throat. A dark and thrillingly horrible adventure into the realms of the unthinkable.” —The Guardian

screenings.title: Blade Runner: The Final Cut
screenings.description: While so many special effects spectacles are lost in time like tears in the rain, Blade Runner remains the template for imagining the neon-wreathed downer of the future, every bit as influential in its vision as was Fritz Lang’s Metropolis over a half century before. Working from a novel by cult writer Philip K. Dick to create a film that would become the gold standard for sci-fi noir, director Scott shares credit here with “visual futurist” Syd Mead’s design concepts and synth pioneer Vangelis’s atmospheric score.

Sweden’s most popular export before the Volvo, in her final screen role, plays a world-renowned concert pianist who returns home to reunite with her now-married daughter (Liv Ullmann), long a distant second to her mother’s career ambitions, the two women exhuming old resentments and struggling towards reconciliation over the course of an emotionally draining 24 hours. “So unrelenting, so harrowing, that I walked out of the theater on shaking legs.
