screenings.title: Fantasia
screenings.description: Walt Disney (and eleven uncredited directors). 1940, 124 mins. U.S. DCP. Disney put it all on the line for this passion project combining his love of cartoons and classical music. Though the result baffled many in its day, Fantasia went on to be one of the most beloved, influential films of all time. Set to works by Bach, Tchaikovsky, Beethoven, Stravinsky, and more, the wordless, exquisitely hand-drawn segments that make up this ambitious masterpiece constitute a high point in animation. Among the most marvelous sequences is its finale, a diptych of the profane and the sacred juxtaposing Modest Mussorgsky’s frenetic and terrifying “Night on Bald Mountain” and Franz Schubert’s ecstatic hymn “Ave Maria.” The former, set on the diabolical Walpurgis Night, is perhaps cinema’s greatest Halloween party. screenings.title: Paris Was a Woman
screenings.description: Drawing on newly discovered home movies and a rich bounty of archival materials, Schiller’s trailblazing documentary, now marking its 30th anniversary, offers up a vibrant and vivacious evocation of the community of female artists and culturati of all stripes—among their number Gertrude Stein, Alice B. Toklas, Djuna Barnes, and Colette—who called Paris’s Left Bank home in the first decades of the previous century. A film that acts on the viewer like a tonic draught of fresh air, Paris Was a Woman is an enthralling evocation of one of the most storied periods in the history of the City of Light and of an anything-goes bohemian enclave that fostered both personal and creative liberation.

screenings.title: Ivan
screenings.description: In making his first sound film, Dovzhenko proved himself every bit as much an innovator in the realm of the aural as he had been in that of the visual, creating a rich sonic tapestry in this melic ode to the construction of the Dnipro Hydroelectric Station and the men and women conscripted into its accomplishment, among them the eponymous Ukrainian villager. (Some critics, however, observed that Dovzhenko took a little too much pleasure in the doings of Ivan’s antagonist, a layabout kulak who refuses to bust his hump slaving away for the glory of the state.) As influential, arguably, as Earth before it, on the Ukrainian poetic cinema of the 1960s, and an achievement of towering stature.

screenings.title: Ec: October
screenings.description: (OKTYABR)“An imaginary document projected on actual locations, OCTOBER is the Soviet equivalent of the Sistine Chapel – an artist commissioned by the state has represented the sacred origins of the universe. Woodrow Wilson had famously hailed D.W. Griffith’s THE BIRTH OF A NATION (1915) as ‘history written with lightning,’ but Eisenstein’s cosmic newsreel cum theoretical film poem goes beyond THE BIRTH OF A NATION, as well as his own BATTLESHIP POTEMKIN, in drafting the past to serve the requirements of the present. No less than the revolutionaries who made October, Eisenstein understood himself as history’s tool. Thus consecrated to the Bolshevik faith, his OCTOBER is a perfect tautology – it clarifies and improves on history in the service of objective historical necessity.” –J. screenings.title: Once Upon a Time in China
screenings.description: No one wields a ’Scope frame with quite the same flexibility and dynamism as Hark, and the spectacular, Sergio Leone–inspired Once Upon a Time in China—perhaps the crucial film of the 1990s wuxia revival—shows Hark at his most flamboyant, keeping up with the human whirlwind that is Jet Li, here in the role of physician, martial artist, and 19th-century Cantonese folk hero Wong Fei-hung, who’s pitted against unscrupulous gangsters, human traffickers from the West, and his inconvenient feelings for “13th Aunt” Rosamund Kwan. Showstopping set pieces come fast and furious en route to a shoot-the-works shipboard finale; a monumental work of kinetic cinema.

screenings.title: Poem of the Sea
screenings.description: Based on a script left behind by Dovzhenko at his death, Poem of the Sea was finally filmed by his widow, Solntseva, a formidable filmmaker in her own right, her stated intention to work wholly “in accordance with Dovzhenko’s artistic conception, putting aside every trace of my own individual vision.” A companion piece of sorts to Ivan, likewise dealing with the construction of a dam and its impact on the surrounding countryside—in particular one soon-to-be-submerged village, birthplace of one General Fedorchenko (Boris Livanov), whose arrival for a visit in its final days stirs long-dormant memories. The feat of civil engineering documented here is the Kakhovka Hydroelectric Power Plant, opened in 1956 and destroyed by Russian forces in 2023, with catastrophic ecological results.

screenings.title: The Red Violin + Live Performance | Instruments of Desire
screenings.description: Following the success of 1993’s Thirty Two Short Films About Glenn Gould, director François Girard and co-writer Don McKellar reunited to tell the story of The Red Violin, tracing the titular instrument’s journey from its creation in 17th-century Italy to an auction in 1990s Montreal–and the various musicians and owners it bewitches along the way. Girard mounts a handsome production with location shooting across five countries, from China to Austria, and Samuel L. Jackson shines as Charles Morritz, a fussy instrument appraiser who falls under the violin’s spell while decoding its secrets. Composer John Corigliano won the Academy Award for Best Original Score, and violinist Joshua Bell performed all of the solos in the film.

screenings.title: Rosalyn Drexler: Who Does She Think She Is?
screenings.image: https://anthologyfilmarchives.org/uploads/Who Does She Think She Is_Still 1 copy.jpg
screenings.description: Rosalyn Drexler (1926-2025) was a category-defying creative force. Over the course of her multidecade career, she worked as a painter (creating some of the first examples of Pop art), a novelist, an Obie-award-winning playwright, a film critic, an occasional nightclub singer, and briefly, a professional wrestler.The documentary WHO DOES SHE THINK SHE IS? (1975) provides a window into Drexler’s extraordinary creative universe. Set against the backdrop of the lost artistic demimonde of 20th-century New York, the film – directed by Patricia Lewis Jaffe and Gaby Rodgers – shows the artist rehearsing her madcap cabaret performances, cooking for her family in her art-strewn Manhattan apartment, and speaking candidly about her art, writing, and life. As Newsweek critic Jack Kroll remarks in the film, “[Drexler’s] essential insight is that people and things are completely insane, and she speaks from inside the whale.”The documentary will be accompanied by never-before-seen home movies shot by Drexler and her husband Sherman in the 1940-50s, as well as a panel discussion. The screening coincides with a major exhibition of her work from the 1960s at Garth Greenan Gallery at 25 Greene Street; for more info about the exhibition visit: https://www.garthgreenan.com/ CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Wildwood in 35mm
screenings.description: Wildwood is a handcrafted epic fantasy that transports audiences into a secret, dangerously alive world. A girl’s desperate quest to save her baby brother unfolds into a spectacular, high-stakes adventure through a forbidden forest full of enchanted creatures, endearing allies, and formidable adversaries—where an entire hidden realm hangs in the balance. In an era of automation, LAIKA delivers its most ambitious and globally accessible film yet—a bold fusion of human-crafted artistry and cinematic storytelling from the makers of Coraline.

screenings.title: Fallen Angels by Noël Coward
screenings.description: Sparkling, dizzying, and deliciously potent, Fallen Angels, Noël Coward’s champagne-fresh comedy of bad manners, shocked and delighted audiences at its 1925 premiere. Two upper-class wives, their husbands away for the day, share a few toasts to their pre-marital dalliances—with the same man, who just may be en route from France to visit. Old rivalries and past scandals bubble to the surface in this intoxicating romp from one of theatre’s comedy masters. Starring Golden Globe-winner Rose Byrne (If I Had Legs I’d Kick You) and Tony Award winner Kelli O’Hara (The King and I), with Tracee Chimo, Mark Consuelos (making his Broadway debut), Christopher Fitzgerald and Aasif Mandvi, this new Roundabout Theatre and Tony Award-winning production of ‘pure escapist fun’ (The New York Times) was filmed live on stage at Broadway’s Todd Haimes Theatre and now comes to the big screen.

screenings.title: First We Bombed New Mexico - the Aftermath
screenings.description: An inspiring New Mexico Latina cancer survivor and businesswoman leads a fight for acknowledgement and compensation for New Mexicans – mostly Latino and Native American - who got multigenerational cancers from Oppenheimer’s Trinity Bomb. An early release of this film created the momentum that led to Congress finally last year awarding billions of dollars in compensation to harmed New Mexicans. Now Tina Cordova has broadened her mission and is fighting for the world’s still ignored victims of nuclear radiation – and for a worldwide ban on nuclear weapons. Tina is a candidate for the Nobel Peace Prize. This film inspires others to keep fighting for social justice and to be seen and heard in a bleak moment when change is needed.

screenings.title: Persona: 60th Anniversary Screening (Co-presented with NewFest)
screenings.description: Dir. Ingmar Bergman. 1966. 82 mins. Sweden. DCP. “If looked at through the right queer lens, Bergman’s Persona could be among the most penetrating break-up movies ever made.” With his landmark drama Persona, which celebrates its 60th anniversary this year, Ingmar Bergman reached new heights of visual poetry. Liv Ullmann, in her first of many legendary collaborations with Bergman, plays a stage actor who has inexplicably gone silent. Bibi Andersson is equally mesmerizing as the garrulous young nurse caring for her at a remote island cottage. Isolated together, the women perform a mysterious spiritual and emotional transference in a scene that has come to influence generations of filmmaking. Shot by the great Sven Nykvist, Persona remains a penetrating, dreamlike work of profound psychological depth that has long been discussed as a breakthrough tale of unspoken love. The Museum is pleased to co-present this masterpiece on the big screen with NewFest, New York’s Largest Queer Film Fest. Purchase tickets through NewFest’s website. Co-presented with:

screenings.title: Music Video Mischief with director Nigel Dick
screenings.description: 6:30–8:00 p.m. The art and style of rock music videos from the mid 1980s through the early 2000s—the choreography, the fashion, the swooning looks!—defined an era for millennials and GenX. Join us in the Bartos Screening Room to see a selection of ebullient music videos from director Nigel Dick. They include Britney Spears’s iconic “Baby One More Time” and Oasis’s “Wonderwall,” plus videos featuring Cher, Celine Dion, Tears for Fears, Guns N’ Roses, Alice Cooper, Def Leppard, and plenty of surprises, too! These videos show some of the chaos and charm of the era. This free screening will be followed by a conversation with Nigel Dick about the making of these classics and a book signing of Dick’s Music Video Mischief: Ozzy to Britney, Oasis to Gn’R, McCartney to Cher: a lifetime of rock and chaos (2026, Trouser Press Books), available for sale in the MoMI Shop (store closes at 8:00 p.m.). Free with RSVP. Special Guest After a brief stint busking in the Paris Metro, Nigel Dick got his start in the music business at London’s upstart Stiff label in the late ’70s. He began a career as a music video director; ultimately working with hundreds of stars, including Oasis, Ozzy Osbourne, Cher, Paul McCartney, Guns n’ Roses, Toto, Britney Spears, Celine Dion, Alice Cooper, Def Leppard, Alice in Chains, and Tears for Fears. If you’ve ever watched MTV, you’ve seen his work. He has directed more than 450 music videos and 35+ documentaries and feature films. He has won three MTV awards, two Billboard Awards, three MVPA awards and one Brit award. His videos have been nominated for a further 21 MTV awards, 26 Much Music Awards, and a Grammy. His book Music Video Mischief is out on Trouser Press Books September 15.

screenings.title: Nosferatu + Live Score
screenings.description: Nosferatu + Live Score by the Andrew Alden Ensemble The vampire film that started them all gets its shadow back. The Andrew Alden Ensemble performs an original score live beneath F.W. Murnau’s 1922 landmark — the New York chamber group whose violin, cello, keys, drums, and voice sit somewhere between contemporary classical and rock, writing music built for the room rather than the recording booth: immediate, physical, and made for this film alone. On screen, Count Orlok (Max Schreck) uncoils out of the Carpathians — all talons and teeth and rat-borne plague — and crosses the sea toward a town that cannot wake from him. A hundred years later the images still crawl.

screenings.title: Bram Stoker’s Dracula
screenings.description: Dir. Francis Ford Coppola. 1992, 128 mins. U.S. 35mm. With Gary Oldman, Winona Ryder, Anthony Hopkins, Sadie Frost, Keanu Reeves, Tom Waits. In adapting the original Victorian-era Gothic vampire novel, Coppola pulled out all the stops and then some. For his rendition of the Dracula story, Coppola produced a quirky, idiosyncratic, and over-the-top cascade of lush and violent horror imagery that was, miraculously, a box-office smash. Working with brilliantly self-imposed limitations (all practical effects that would have been possible in the silent era); cramming every frame with monumental sets and matte paintings; and directing Oldman in one of his finest performances as the devilishly romantic Transylvanian count, Coppola created a film so sensational that even the notoriously horror-averse Academy Awards honored it three times, for makeup, sound effects, and Eiko Ishioka’s dazzling costumes. screenings.title: Vampyr + Live Score
screenings.description: Carl Theodor Dreyer’s 1932 fever dream is less a horror film than a nightmare filmed at the moment of waking — fog, drifting shadows, a scythe, a burial seen from inside the coffin. The Andrew Alden Ensemble scores it live with violin, electric guitar, piano, synthesizers, and percussion, the New York group’s music moving with the film’s logic of dread rather than against it. A young traveler, Allan Gray (Julian West), arrives in a riverside village held under the spell of a vampire, and the world begins to come loose at the edges. Dreyer made it as sound cinema was being born and produced something stranger than either silence or speech; performed with a live original score, it turns stranger still.

Widely considered one of the scariest films ever made, The Exorcist has shocked and fascinated generations of viewers. screenings.title: An American Werewolf in London
screenings.description: Dir. John Landis. 1981, 97 mins. U.S. DCP. With David Naughton, Griffin Dunne, Jenny Agutter. The rare humor-tinged horror that manages to be entirely terrifying and quite funny, Landis’s film follows two American backpackers whose destinies are changed forever when they decide to stray from the roads while traveling across rural England. After being bitten by a strange furry animal, David Kessler (Naughton) wakes up in a London hospital and finds himself plagued by ominous dreams and foreboding ghosts telling him to beware the next full moon. Rick Baker’s eye-popping practical makeup effects (which won an Oscar the first year the Academy added a makeup category) enhance this marvelous dark comedy that still has the power to make audiences scream and giggle. Griffin Dunne appears in an unforgettable supporting role as David’s friend, whose death can’t stop him from trying to hang out. screenings.title: Fugs Film!
screenings.description: Formed in late 1964 by Ed Sanders and Tuli Kupferberg, alongside drummer Ken Weaver – anarchic East Village beat poets who could barely play their instruments – The Fugs are credited as the first true underground band. Their lo-fi folk music could be challenging and weird but they had a knack for catchy pop songs, such as “Supergirl” and ‘Slum Goddess”. One of the most crucial figures in countercultural history, Sanders founded the Peace Eye bookstore and the arts journal “F*** You: A Magazine of the Arts”, and, among other late-1960s antics, attempted to levitate the Pentagon and staged a funeral for flower power in San Francisco. Chuck Smith’s vital documentary features eye-popping archival footage and interviews with Sanders, Aline & R. Crumb, Lenny Kaye, Penny Arcade, Jeffrey Lewis, and many others, to tell the story of NYC’s original punks.The screening will be followed by a Q&A with Penny Arcade, Steven Taylor and other participants from the film!CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: The Wolf Man
screenings.description: Dir. Curt Siodmak. 1941, 70 mins. DCP. With Lon Chaney Jr., Claude Rains, Evelyn Ankers, Maria Ouspenskaya, Ralph Bellamy, Patric Knowles, Warren William, Bela Lugosi. Happy homecomings and family reconciliations take a ghastly turn when Larry Talbot is attacked by and kills a wolf during an evening out, though only a man’s body is found after the tragedy. The mystery deepens when Larry learns that this man was a werewolf, and now, when the wolfbane blooms and the autumn moon is bright, he too will make the same transformation. The Wolf Man is the finest horror movie of Universal’s monster revival in the 1940s, celebrated for its spectacular makeup effects by Jack Pierce and Lon Chaney Jr.’s tortured turn in the title role. screenings.title: Fallen Angels by Noël Coward
screenings.description: Sparkling, dizzying, and deliciously potent, Fallen Angels, Noël Coward’s champagne-fresh comedy of bad manners, shocked and delighted audiences at its 1925 premiere. Two upper-class wives, their husbands away for the day, share a few toasts to their pre-marital dalliances—with the same man, who just may be en route from France to visit. Old rivalries and past scandals bubble to the surface in this intoxicating romp from one of theatre’s comedy masters. Starring Golden Globe-winner Rose Byrne (If I Had Legs I’d Kick You) and Tony Award winner Kelli O’Hara (The King and I), with Tracee Chimo, Mark Consuelos (making his Broadway debut), Christopher Fitzgerald and Aasif Mandvi, this new Roundabout Theatre and Tony Award-winning production of ‘pure escapist fun’ (The New York Times) was filmed live on stage at Broadway’s Todd Haimes Theatre and now comes to the big screen.

screenings.title: Magic
screenings.description: Dir. Richard Attenborough. 1978, 107 mins. U.S. 35mm. With Anthony Hopkins, Ann-Margret, Burgess Meredith, Ed Lauter. In this sinister cult classic, a brilliantly unbalanced Anthony Hopkins plays Charles “Corky” Withers, a failed magician turned ventriloquist who begins to show symptoms of psychosis—and allows his dummy, the foul-mouthed “Fats,” to take over his life. Is he shuttling head-first into a mental crackup? Or does the mean-spirited Fats truly have a mind of his own? Genuinely unsettling, this shadowy, emotionally gripping thriller was infamous for its 1970s TV spots, which scarred a generation of unsuspecting kids, but the film is diabolically effective in every way, and features a stellar cast, including a touching Ann-Margret as his love interest. screenings.title: On the Relentless Destruction of Beauty: Short Housing Films + Q&A
screenings.description: On The Relentless Destruction of Beauty features artist studios, communized parks, and residential buildings as spaces produced through—and for—collective creativity, labor, and cohabitation. Spanning the 1960s to the present, the program traces the ways everyday acts of living and making come into conflict with capital’s logic of private property, which seeks to empty such spaces of life in the pursuit of profit. Across these four films, however, the home emerges not as a commodity to be exchanged—nor as an asset to be valued through speculation and dispossession—but as a site of ongoing creative struggle.

screenings.description: Paranoid Brigadier General Jack D. Ripper of Burpelson Air Force Base, believing that fluoridation of the American water supply is a Soviet plot to poison the U.S. populace, is able to deploy through a back door mechanism a nuclear attack on the Soviet Union without the knowledge of his superiors, including the Chair of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, General Buck Turgidson, and President Merkin Muffley. Only Ripper knows the code to recall the B-52 bombers and he has shut down communication in and out of Burpelson as a measure to protect this attack. screenings.title: Who Killed Alex Odeh?
screenings.description: In October 1985, Santa Ana, California was shaken by a brazen act of political violence when Palestinian American Alex Odeh, a beloved teacher and community leader, was killed by a tripwire bomb planted in his office. Despite substantial evidence and identified suspects, the case was never solved. Who Killed Alex Odeh? reopens the mystery, tracking a renewed investigation in real time as new leads emerge, long-buried records come to light, and the forces behind a political assassination are finally confronted. In English, Arabic and Hebrew with English subtitles.

screenings.title: Ec: Nanook of the North
screenings.description: Flaherty’s pioneering ethnographic film depicts the struggle for survival of Inuit hunter Nanook and his family. Though rife with staged scenes, anachronisms, and an indulgence in the myth of the “noble savage” (Nanook was in fact an Inuit man named Allakariallak, who hunted not with harpoons and spears but with a rifle), NANOOK OF THE NORTH is a work of great lyricism, simplicity of design, and genuine affection for its protagonists, and its force is undiminished almost 100 years after it was made.

screenings.title: Suspiria
screenings.description: Both the pinnacle of his career and the giallo subgenre, Dario Argento’s Suspiria ranks in the pantheon of the greatest horror movies of all time, and with damn good reason. Masterfully employing dream logic (the script was co-written by then wife Daria Nicolodi) and gloriously garish lighting techniques, the film is a true modern fairy tale that tells the story of a ballet student (Jessica Harper) who transfers to a German dance academy only to find it is run by a coven of murderous witches. Argento’s command of shock and suspense is on full display in every blood-soaked scene, but the true secret weapon of Suspiria is the unbelievably scary and propulsive score by the prog rock band Goblin. It all adds up to that rare witches brew: the perfect horror experience.

screenings.title: Ec: Man of Aran
screenings.description: Flaherty’s third major film portrays the lives of a family of fisher folk on the Aran Islands off the coast of Galway, Ireland. Flaherty selected the location and subjects because of their isolation as the westernmost outpost of European civilization. In addition, the daily struggle between the islanders and the sea perfectly suited his interests and concerns. The scenes at sea are breathtaking.“His passionate devotion to the portrayal of human gesture and of a man’s fight for his family makes the film an incomparable account of human dignity. Better than anyone, Flaherty knew how to show the true face of Man.” –Georges Sadoul

screenings.title: Halloween
screenings.description: Credited, rightfully, as the film that kickstarted the “slasher” subgenre, Carpenter’s 1978 Halloween is a masterwork of building tension, an exercise in mood and suspense that takes its cues from Hitchcock, unlike most of the 80s gorefests it would inspire. The film’s key innovation – besides the indelibly terrifying image of the blank-faced “shape” aka Michael Myers – is setting it in an innocuous American suburb; there’s nowhere, not even a nice middle class home, where the viewer is safe. Jamie Lee Curtis makes her scream queen debut as one of several babysitters being stalked by a masked, escaped mental patient on Halloween night, her only savior being the patient’s maniacally driven doctor, played with gusto by the great Donald Pleasance. But the secret weapon of Halloween is the score – composed by Carpenter himself – a tinkling, off-meter piano figure that continues to haunt long after the final unsettling frame. A Halloween season perennial.

screenings.title: Suspiria
screenings.description: Both the pinnacle of his career and the giallo subgenre, Dario Argento’s Suspiria ranks in the pantheon of the greatest horror movies of all time, and with damn good reason. Masterfully employing dream logic (the script was co-written by then wife Daria Nicolodi) and gloriously garish lighting techniques, the film is a true modern fairy tale that tells the story of a ballet student (Jessica Harper) who transfers to a German dance academy only to find it is run by a coven of murderous witches. Argento’s command of shock and suspense is on full display in every blood-soaked scene, but the true secret weapon of Suspiria is the unbelievably scary and propulsive score by the prog rock band Goblin. It all adds up to that rare witches brew: the perfect horror experience.

[…] A dream-like quality permeates the intense realism of the images; a surrealist intent – akin to Buñuel’s slitting of the eyeball in UN CHIEN ANDALOU – is discernible in this anti-bourgeois film. Like all Genet’s early work, the entire film is, in effect, a single onanistic fantasy, filled with desperate frustration and sensuous nostalgia.” –Amos Vogel, FILM AS A SUBVERSIVE ART“There’s no smoke without fire; UN CHANT D’AMOUR is a communion in which Genet takes us into the prison in order to liberate us from it.” –Derek JarmanTotal running time: ca. 50 min.CLICK HERE TO BOOK TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Halloween
screenings.description: Credited, rightfully, as the film that kickstarted the “slasher” subgenre, Carpenter’s 1978 Halloween is a masterwork of building tension, an exercise in mood and suspense that takes its cues from Hitchcock, unlike most of the 80s gorefests it would inspire. The film’s key innovation – besides the indelibly terrifying image of the blank-faced “shape” aka Michael Myers – is setting it in an innocuous American suburb; there’s nowhere, not even a nice middle class home, where the viewer is safe. Jamie Lee Curtis makes her scream queen debut as one of several babysitters being stalked by a masked, escaped mental patient on Halloween night, her only savior being the patient’s maniacally driven doctor, played with gusto by the great Donald Pleasance. But the secret weapon of Halloween is the score – composed by Carpenter himself – a tinkling, off-meter piano figure that continues to haunt long after the final unsettling frame. A Halloween season perennial.

screenings.title: The Draughtsman's Contract + Live Performance | Instruments of Desire
screenings.description: Set in a richly exaggerated 17th-century England, Peter Greenaway’s sumptuous and sensuously charged brainteaser catapulted him to the forefront of international art cinema. Adorned with intricate wordplay, extravagant costumes and opulent photography, Greenaway’s first narrative feature weaves a labyrinthine mystery around the maxim “draw what you see, not what you know.” An aristocratic wife (Janet Suzman) commissions a young, cocksure draughtsman (Anthony Higgins) to sketch her husband’s property while he is away—in exchange for a fee, room and board, and one sexual favor for each of the twelve drawings. As the draughtsman becomes more entrenched in the devious schemings in this seemingly idyllic country home, curious details emerge in his drawings that may reveal a murder.

screenings.title: Tár + Live Performance | Instruments of Desire
screenings.description: From writer-producer-director Todd Field comes TÁR, starring Cate Blanchett as Lydia Tár, the celebrated chief conductor of the Berlin Philharmonic. We meet Tár at the height of her career, as she’s preparing both a book launch and a much-anticipated live recording of Mahler’s Fifth Symphony. Over the ensuing weeks, her life and career unravel as allegations of misconduct erode her carefully cultivated public image. The result is a searing examination of artistic authority, institutional politics, and the blurred boundary between mentorship and exploitation.

screenings.title: Orfeo
screenings.description: In the classic Greek tragedy, a snake bites Eurydice on her wedding day, and her new husband, Orpheus, travels to the Underworld to bring her back. Virgilio Villoresi’s expressionistic adaptation of the tale is based on Dino Buzzati’s 1969 Poema a fumetti, Italy ‘s first graphic novel. The film is a modern reimagining with an aesthetic untethered from reality: a kaleidoscopic journey through time and place, reflecting on art, love, mystery, eroticism, melancholy, life, and death.
